summary.text: The Saturn V was a retired American super heavy-lift rocket that NASA developed under the Apollo program for human exploration of the Moon.
It had three liquid-fuelled stages, and thirteen were launched between 1967 and 1973, nine of them sending 24 astronauts toward the Moon.
It was the first launch vehicle to carry humans beyond low Earth orbit, and it holds the record for the largest payload capacity to low Earth orbit, 140,000 kg.

facts.label: First-stage engines
facts.value: Five F-1 engines, built by Rocketdyne

facts.label: Designed at
facts.value: Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama

items.prompt: Planners wanted a crewed launch after as few test flights as possible. Which testing approach did they choose?

options.label: Test each major component in its own flight, one at a time
Fly the first test with complete versions of all three stages
Fly the upper stage alone many times on smaller rockets
Skip uncrewed tests by putting astronauts on the first flight

items.explain: The rocket was tested in an all-up fashion, so the first flight included all three stages, and testing everything at once meant far fewer flights before a crewed launch.

items.prompt: Why did the Saturn rockets get that name?

options.label: The five engines on the first stage were arranged like the planet's rings
NASA named it for a Roman god picked by its Apollo managers
It was named for the company that built the first stage
The designs grew out of earlier Jupiter rockets, named for another planet

items.explain: The Saturn family evolved from the earlier Jupiter vehicles, which were named after the planet Jupiter.

items.prompt: NASA weighed flying a three-man spacecraft straight to the Moon, landing it whole and flying it home. What made that option hard?

It needed engines that burned a different kind of fuel

items.explain: A direct ascent would need an extremely large rocket to land directly on the surface with enough fuel to fly back to Earth.

items.prompt: Von Braun's team in the US at first had little to work with. What shifted the government's effort?

options.label: The Army found a cheaper way to build rockets in wooden workshops
His magazine articles convinced Congress to fund a Moon rocket

items.explain: When the Soviets launched Sputnik 1 atop an R-7 ICBM, the American Army and government began putting more effort into sending Americans into space.

paragraphs.heading: The Moon rocket
paragraphs.text: The Saturn V was a super heavy-lift American rocket that NASA developed under the Apollo program so that people could explore the Moon. It had three stages, ran on liquid fuel and was rated to carry humans. Between 1967 and 1973 thirteen of them lifted off, all from Launch Complex 39 at Kennedy Space Center. Nine of those flights, from Apollo 8 to Apollo 17, sent a total of 24 astronauts toward the Moon.

paragraphs.heading: Records
paragraphs.text: It was the first launch vehicle to take people beyond low Earth orbit; the only other one to do so is the Space Launch System, or SLS, on the Artemis II flyby of the Moon in 2026. It still holds the record for the most payload to low Earth orbit, 140,000 kg, a figure that counts the third stage with the leftover propellant used to send the Apollo spacecraft to the Moon. At launch it gave 34.5 meganewtons of thrust, ranking fourth among all rockets and second among those that have carried people, behind SLS.

paragraphs.heading: Three stages
paragraphs.text: All of the engines were made by Rocketdyne. Boeing built the first stage, the S-IC, with five F-1 engines, which are still the most powerful single-chamber liquid-fuel engines ever made. North American Aviation built the second stage, the S-II, with five J-2 engines. Douglas Aircraft Company built the third stage, the S-IVB, with a single J-2. IBM and NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center designed the instrument unit.

paragraphs.heading: The people behind it
paragraphs.text: The rocket was designed at the Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama. George Mueller managed the program, while the technical design was led by scientists brought over from Nazi Germany, above all Wernher von Braun. Von Braun came to the United States in September 1945 under Operation Paperclip, which brought more than 1,600 German rocket engineers and technicians to work for the US government after World War II. His group had already built the first American launch vehicles, the Redstone rockets.

paragraphs.heading: From Jupiter to Saturn
paragraphs.text: In 1957 the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, and the US Army and government began trying harder to get Americans into space before the Soviets. The Army turned to von Braun's team, which had made the Jupiter rockets. Von Braun saw Jupiter as a prototype for the coming Saturn rockets and called it "an infant Saturn". The new family was named after the planet Saturn because it grew out of the Jupiter rockets, which bore the name of the planet Jupiter.

paragraphs.heading: Testing it all at once
paragraphs.text: NASA approved the design, then called the C-5, on January 25, 1962, and it was named the Saturn V in February 1963. Rather than test each major part on separate flights, NASA chose all-up testing: the very first test flight would carry complete versions of all three stages. Testing everything together meant far fewer test flights were needed before a crew could fly. The first launch came on the Apollo 4 test flight in November 1967.

paragraphs.heading: The last flight
paragraphs.text: The final Saturn V launch put Skylab into orbit, the first American space station, which had been converted from a Saturn V third stage. Two more Saturn Vs, meant for Apollo 19 and 20, were built but never used.
